newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul unionists leave church, opposition backs down.
newsitem.headline: Seoul unionists leave church, opposition backs down.

text.p: South Korean strike leaders abandoned their tent headquarters at Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral on Friday as the government and opposition groped towards compromise over a controversial new labour law.
With little fanfare, shaven-headed leaders of the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions left behind the ramshackle tent from where they directed almost a month of stoppages.
But leader Kwon Young-kil insisted it was a tactical move and he vowed his outlawed union would fight on against the law.

Nevertheless, the main opposition National Congress for New Politics softened its stand and said it was now prepared to debate the new law in parliament if the government apologised for its forced passage.
The party had previously said it and a smaller opposition party would hold dialogue with the government only if the legislation was first revoked.

In a move likely to further ease tension, police freed four unionists from Halla Heavy Industries' shipyard after prosecutors dropped charges against them, a prosecution official said. All arrested union leaders are now free.
The official added that 15 outstanding arrest warrants for Kwon and other heads of the confederation would be scrapped.
Kwon embraced Roman Catholic priests before quietly slipping out of the cathedral with six deputies in several cars.
The cathedral became a symbol of worker anger at the law and the focus of a round-the-clock media stakeout after prosecutors issued warrants for the arrest of strike leaders.

Unionists pitched their plastic tent on the cathedral's icy grounds on December 26, the day the ruling New Korea Party rammed the labour bill through parliament in a dawn session while opposition deputies slept.
Political analysts said South Korea's industrial strife was now largely a political affair that could be solved only through dialogue, mainly between the ruling party and opposition.

The confederation on Saturday decided to limit industrial action to one day a week, on Wednesdays, in protest at the law, which makes it easier for companies to sack workers, replace strikers and adjust working hours.
On other days there have been no work disruptions.
Kwon's exit from the church follows a peace offer on Tuesday by President Kim Young-sam, who ordered the suspension of arrest warrants.
In a meeting with opposition leaders, Kim agreed to reopen parliamentary debate over the law after admitting it had caused public anxiety and damaged the economy.
But Kwon said the fight was not over.

"We are not softening our will to fight. We are moving to a bigger place from our small confines here to stage a more forceful struggle," he said. Another confederation official said Kwon would head for the group's office in the capital.
Kim, who had previously ruled out a revision or compromise, has said dumping the law would be unconstitutional.
The union move out of the church, which offered protection from arrest, should help ease friction between the government and union leaders, analysts said.
However, Labour Minister Jin Nyum said on Thursday the government would no longer tolerate illegal strikes. He did not specify what measures would be taken against strikers.
The climbdown by the National Congress followed fierce criticism of its hardline stance by the ruling party.
"If the government apologises for ramming the law through parliament we are willing to start talks over the law," Park Hong-yeop, National Congress deputy spokesman, told Reuters.
"We will interpret an apology as returning to square one, although the government would probably see it as only revising the law. We will leave that to the Korean people to judge."
Park said his party expected the apology to come from the speaker of the National Assembly.
